title: Wh-questions with Who, Whom, Which, How and Whose
summary: Form precise questions about people, selections, descriptions and possession. Distinguish subject and object who, formal whom after prepositions, restricted which choices, usual singular subject-question agreement, how versus what, and possessive whose in direct and embedded questions.
learningObjectives: Choose who, whom or which according to whether the question targets a subject, an object or a defined group of people or things.
Handle the usual singular agreement of subject who/what and recognise plural complements and echo-question exceptions.
Distinguish how questions about condition, manner or preferences from what questions about details, descriptions and hypothetical outcomes.
Use whose as an independent pronoun or determiner, with appropriate preposition placement in formal and informal questions.

explanation.heading: Who, whom and their grammatical roles
explanation.body: Who can ask about the subject, object or complement of a clause. Formal whom is mainly used for people as objects and is especially natural immediately after a fronted preposition: to whom was the note addressed? It is not the ordinary subject form; who organised the event? cannot normally become whom organised the event? In everyday speech, who is common instead of object whom, particularly with the preposition at the end.
explanation.example: To whom did the chairperson hand the revised agenda?

explanation.heading: Which selects from a group
explanation.body: Which identifies a person or thing from an identifiable set. It is particularly natural before one or ones and before of + a defined group: which of the shortlisted candidates is available? Which can also ask about a particular class of people, while who may be possible when the focus is a person rather than a choice. Avoid who of the shortlisted candidates: which of is the conventional pattern for an explicit selection.
explanation.example: Which of the two translators will present the findings?

explanation.heading: Agreement and the difference between subjects and complements
explanation.body: When who or what itself is the subject, a singular verb is generally used even when several people or things may be named in the answer: who manages the schedules? and what is there to see? A plural verb may appear in echo questions when a plural item has just been mentioned or the question targets a coordinated subject. When who or what is a complement after be, the verb agrees with the actual plural subject: who are those people? and what are the consequences?
explanation.example: Who is responsible for issuing the passes, and who are those visitors?

explanation.heading: How and what ask different kinds of questions
explanation.body: How was the concert? seeks a general assessment; what was the concert like? can request a similar broad description, while what did you enjoy about the concert? asks for details. How do you like your coffee? asks about a preference, not the reasons you appreciate it. What if introduces a hypothetical consequence, while what is it called? asks for a name. Both how about and what about can introduce suggestions or follow-up questions, but the wording of other how and what constructions is not freely interchangeable.
explanation.example: How do you like your tea, and what do you like about this blend?

explanation.heading: Whose for possession and responsibility
explanation.body: Whose can stand alone as a pronoun (whose are these?) or modify a noun (whose folder is this?). It signals a person associated with or responsible for an object, not only legal ownership. Whose is distinct from who’s, a contraction of who is or who has. Formal questions may front a required preposition before whose: in whose office was the document found? Informal versions may strand it: whose office was the document found in? Where there is no main verb requiring a preposition, do not append one to a short question such as whose office?
explanation.example: Whose notes did the facilitator collect at the end of the workshop?

comparisons.title: Formal preposition fronting versus conversational placement

left.label: Formal object whom
left.example: With whom did the director discuss the plans?
left.note: Whom follows the preposition when the object is explicitly fronted.

right.label: Conversational object who
right.example: Who did the director discuss the plans with?
right.note: Who is a natural object form with the preposition left at the end.

left.label: How + preference
left.example: How do you like your coffee?
left.note: The answer may be strong, black, sweet or another preparation preference.

right.label: What + valued feature
right.example: What do you like about this coffee?
right.note: The answer identifies qualities such as its aroma or flavour.

examples.note: Who is the subject of designed, so whom is inappropriate.

examples.sentence: Which of the five applications arrived first?
examples.note: Which of refers to a choice within a stated group.

examples.sentence: What is there to explore near the harbour?
examples.note: Subject what normally combines with singular is in an existential question.

examples.sentence: Who are the two researchers beside the poster?
examples.note: Who functions as a complement, and plural researchers requires are.

examples.sentence: Whose umbrella is leaning against the counter?
examples.note: Whose modifies umbrella; it is not the contraction who’s.

commonMistakes.why: The interrogative word is the grammatical subject of designed; use who, not object whom.

commonMistakes.incorrect: Who of the shortlisted volunteers knows the procedure?
commonMistakes.correct: Which of the shortlisted volunteers knows the procedure?
commonMistakes.why: Which of identifies an individual within an explicit group.

commonMistakes.incorrect: What are there to see in this village?
commonMistakes.correct: What is there to see in this village?
commonMistakes.why: What as the subject of this existential expression normally takes singular is.

commonMistakes.incorrect: Who’s jacket has been left in the library?
commonMistakes.correct: Whose jacket has been left in the library?
commonMistakes.why: Whose is the possessive determiner; who’s means who is or who has.

studyTips: Label the interrogative word as subject, object, complement or determiner before choosing who, whom or whose.
Compare closed-choice which of the group questions with open who questions, then note whether singular agreement is required.
Practise paired prompts: how was it? / what was it like? and how do you like it? / what do you like about it? Explain the difference in information requested.

exercises.prompt: ___ is leading the seminar this afternoon? Choose the interrogative pronoun functioning as subject.
exercises.feedback: Who is the subject of is leading; whom is an object form and whose is possessive.

exercises.prompt: To ___ did you send the recommendation? Choose the formal object form when the recipient is a person.
exercises.feedback: A fronted preposition addressed to a person conventionally takes whom.

exercises.prompt: ___ of the five paintings is the earliest? Choose the natural word for a defined set.
exercises.feedback: Which of introduces a choice within the specified five paintings.

exercises.prompt: You want to learn which features a colleague values in a new job. Which question asks for these details?
choices: How do you like your new job?
What do you like about your new job?
What is your new job like?
exercises.feedback: What do you like about ... invites particular valued aspects rather than only a broad impression.

exercises.prompt: ___ of these two chairs would you choose? Supply the single word that introduces a selection.
exercises.feedback: Which of asks for a choice within the two chairs.

exercises.prompt: ___ created the original design? Supply the subject interrogative pronoun.
exercises.feedback: Who functions as the subject of created.

exercises.prompt: ___ headphones were left in the meeting room? Supply a possessive interrogative determiner.
exercises.feedback: Whose modifies headphones, indicating their owner or responsible person.

exercises.prompt: ___ is there to explore in the old quarter? Supply the single subject question word.
exercises.feedback: What normally takes singular is in this existential subject question.

exercises.prompt: Correct the subject-question form: Whom is delivering the opening lecture?
acceptedAnswers: Who is delivering the opening lecture?
exercises.feedback: The question word is subject of is delivering, so use who.

exercises.prompt: Correct the explicit selection: Who of those three engineers signed the report?
acceptedAnswers: Which of those three engineers signed the report?
exercises.feedback: Which of, not who of, is the usual way to select from a named group.

exercises.prompt: Correct the possessive question: Who’s coat is hanging on that hook?
acceptedAnswers: Whose coat is hanging on that hook?
exercises.feedback: Whose is the possessive determiner before coat.

exercises.prompt: Correct the description question: How was the concert like?
exercises.feedback: With be + like to request a description, use what, not how.

speakingExercises.prompt: Ask about the person who approved the budget. Begin with “Who” and use the past simple.
speakingExercises.feedback: Who is the subject of approved.

speakingExercises.prompt: Ask formally about the recipient of a parcel. Begin “To whom” and include “was the parcel delivered”.
acceptedAnswers: To whom was the parcel delivered?
speakingExercises.feedback: Whom is the object of the fronted preposition to.

speakingExercises.prompt: Ask a colleague to choose between two routes. Use “Which of the two routes” and “do you prefer”.
acceptedAnswers: Which of the two routes do you prefer?
speakingExercises.feedback: Which of identifies an option from a closed set.

speakingExercises.prompt: Ask about the owner of this umbrella. Begin “Whose umbrella” and use a complete be-question.
speakingExercises.feedback: Whose is a possessive determiner before umbrella.

speakingExercises.prompt: Ask for a general assessment of someone’s trip, using how and the past simple.
speakingExercises.feedback: How was asks for a general evaluation.

speakingExercises.prompt: Ask which particular features someone appreciates in their new apartment. Begin “What do you like”.
acceptedAnswers: What do you like about your new apartment?
speakingExercises.feedback: What do you like about ... requests specific positive features.

speakingExercises.prompt: Correct this question aloud: “Whom left the message?”
speakingExercises.feedback: Only who is suitable as the interrogative subject in this question.

speakingExercises.prompt: Produce two full questions in this order. First ask how someone likes their coffee; then ask whose notebook this is. Use exact referents coffee and notebook.
acceptedAnswers: How do you like your coffee? Whose notebook is this?
speakingExercises.feedback: The first question asks about preparation preference; the second asks about possession.

listeningExercises.audioText: Who called the maintenance office? The laboratory assistant called before lunch.
listeningExercises.feedback: The assistant is identified as the subject of called.

listeningExercises.audioText: To whom should we send the updated contract? Send it to the legal adviser, please.
choices: The office from which it was sent.
listeningExercises.feedback: Whom is the person receiving the contract after the preposition to.

listeningExercises.audioText: Which of the two blue jackets is yours? The one with the silver buttons.
listeningExercises.prompt: Transcribe the two words at the start of the selection question.
listeningExercises.feedback: Which of introduces a restricted choice between the jackets.

listeningExercises.audioText: What do you like about the studio? The natural light and the quiet rooms.
listeningExercises.prompt: What information does the first question ask for?
choices: The exact location of the studio.
listeningExercises.feedback: What do you like about elicits appreciated details, here light and quiet rooms.

listeningExercises.audioText: Who are those visitors standing by the entrance? They are the new members of the committee.
choices: Who asks for the identity of the plural subject those visitors.
Whom must always be followed by a plural verb.
Who is always plural, even in subject questions.
listeningExercises.feedback: Who is a complement here; the actual subject those visitors is plural.

listeningExercises.audioText: How do you like your eggs? Poached, with a little salt.
choices: Which aspect of the eggs tastes best.
How the person prefers their eggs prepared.
listeningExercises.feedback: How do you like your eggs asks about the preferred preparation.

listeningExercises.audioText: Whose folder was left on the photocopier? I think it belongs to the trainee.
listeningExercises.prompt: Transcribe the first two words of the possession question.
listeningExercises.feedback: Whose folder identifies a possessor through a determiner plus noun.

listeningExercises.audioText: What was the exhibition like? It was surprisingly engaging.
listeningExercises.prompt: Transcribe the complete five-word opening question.
listeningExercises.feedback: What was ... like requests an overall description or impression.
